claim: Skeletal muscle degeneration is a complication arising from a variety of chronic diseases including advanced cancer.
source: Skeletal muscle degeneration is a complication arising from a variety of chronic diseases including advanced cancer.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established background information.

claim: Pro-inflammatory cytokine TNF-α plays a pivotal role in mediating cancer-related skeletal muscle degeneration.
source: Pro-inflammatory cytokine TNF-α plays a pivotal role in mediating cancer-related skeletal muscle degeneration.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: In human skeletal muscle myotubes (HSMMs), up-regulation of cyclin-dependent kinase 4 (CDK4) and concomitant phosphorylation of Rb was induced by TNF-α treatment.
source: In human skeletal muscle myotubes (HSMMs), up-regulation of cyclin-dependent kinase 4 (CDK4) and concomitant phosphorylation of Rb was induced by TNF-α treatment
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and 1E.

claim: TNF-α treatment results in the translocation of phosphorylated Rb to the cytoplasm.
source: In human skeletal muscle myotubes (HSMMs), up-regulation of cyclin-dependent kinase 4 (CDK4) and concomitant phosphorylation of Rb was induced by TNF-α treatment, resulting in the translocation of phosphorylated Rb to the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1B, 1C, and 1D.

claim: Induced expression of the nuclear exporting signal (NES)-fused form of Rb caused disruption of sarcomeric organization.
source: Moreover, induced expression of the nuclear exporting signal (NES)-fused form of Rb caused disruption of sarcomeric organization.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Mammalian diaphanous-related formin 1 (mDia1) is a binding partner of cytoplasmic Rb.
source: We identified mammalian diaphanous-related formin 1 (mDia1), a potent actin nucleation factor, as a binding partner of cytoplasmic Rb
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data (Figure 7—figure supplement 1) and immunoprecipitation experiments (Figure 7D, 7E).

claim: mDia1 helps maintain the structural integrity of the sarcomere.
source: We identified mammalian diaphanous-related formin 1 (mDia1), a potent actin nucleation factor, as a binding partner of cytoplasmic Rb and found that mDia1 helps maintain the structural integrity of the sarcomere.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that mDia1 depletion disrupts sarcomeric organization (Figure 10) and that constitutively active mDia1 rescues TNF-α-induced sarcomeric disorganization (Figure 9).

claim: Skeletal muscle degeneration is characterized by the progressive depletion of muscle strength.
source: Skeletal muscle degeneration, which is characterized by the progressive depletion of muscle strength, occurs in a variety of chronic diseases including advanced cancer, congestive heart failure, and AIDS (Tisdale, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Tisdale, 2002.

claim: Skeletal muscle degeneration occurs in a variety of chronic diseases including advanced cancer, congestive heart failure, and AIDS.
source: Skeletal muscle degeneration, which is characterized by the progressive depletion of muscle strength, occurs in a variety of chronic diseases including advanced cancer, congestive heart failure, and AIDS (Tisdale, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Tisdale, 2002.

claim: Inflammatory cytokines, particularly TNF-α, have been shown to be key mediators of cancer-related skeletal muscle degeneration.
source: Inflammatory cytokines, particularly TNF-α, have been shown to be key mediators of cancer-related skeletal muscle degeneration (Tisdale, 2002; Seruga et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tisdale, 2002 and Seruga et al., 2008.

claim: Elevated levels of TNF-α precede the onset of cancer-related skeletal muscle degeneration.
source: Elevated levels of TNF-α precede the onset of cancer-related skeletal muscle degeneration and act through several cancer-related signaling pathways such as the p53 and nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) pathways (Guttridge et al., 2000; Cai et al., 2004; Schwarzkopf et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Guttridge et al., 2000; Cai et al., 2004; Schwarzkopf et al., 2006.

claim: TNF-α acts through several cancer-related signaling pathways such as the p53 and nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) pathways.
source: Elevated levels of TNF-α precede the onset of cancer-related skeletal muscle degeneration and act through several cancer-related signaling pathways such as the p53 and nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) pathways (Guttridge et al., 2000; Cai et al., 2004; Schwarzkopf et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Guttridge et al., 2000; Cai et al., 2004; Schwarzkopf et al., 2006.

claim: Retinoblastoma protein (Rb) prevents tumor formation by inducing differentiation, controlling cell-cycle progression, and maintaining genomic stability.
source: Retinoblastoma protein (Rb) prevents tumor formation by inducing differentiation, controlling cell-cycle progression, and maintaining genomic stability (Burkhart and Sage, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Burkhart and Sage, 2008.

claim: Rb forms a transcriptional repressor complex with two protein groups, E2F transcription factors and LXCXE motif-containing proteins.
source: Rb forms a transcriptional repressor complex with two protein groups, E2F transcription factors and LXCXE motif-containing proteins (Halaban, 2005; Burkhart and Sage, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Halaban, 2005 and Burkhart and Sage, 2008.

claim: Rb activity is regulated by sequential phosphorylation on several serine and threonine residues, first by cyclin D/cyclin-dependent kinase 4 (CDK4) and then by cyclin E/CDK2 complexes.
source: Rb activity is regulated by sequential phosphorylation on several serine and threonine residues, first by cyclin D/cyclin-dependent kinase 4 (CDK4) and then by cyclin E/CDK2 complexes (Halaban, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Halaban, 2005.

claim: Serial phosphorylation of Rb induces dissociation of the transcriptional repressor complex, allowing expression of E2F-target genes.
source: This serial phosphorylation of Rb induces dissociation of the transcriptional repressor complex, allowing expression of E2F-target genes, which are required for many cellular processes.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about Rb function.

claim: Loss of Rb function in many cancer cells is frequently caused by aberrant CDK-mediated phosphorylation.
source: Loss of Rb function in many cancer cells is frequently caused by aberrant CDK-mediated phosphorylation (Chau and Wang, 2003; Burkhart and Sage, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chau and Wang, 2003 and Burkhart and Sage, 2008.

claim: Selective CDK inhibition is considered a potentially useful approach for cancer treatment.
source: Consequently, selective CDK inhibition is considered a potentially useful approach for cancer treatment (Malumbres and Barbacid, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Malumbres and Barbacid, 2009.

claim: Inactivation of Rb, which is induced by TNF-α treatment, has been shown to lead to various cellular behaviors including proliferation of vascular smooth muscle cells and apoptosis of fibroblasts and aortic endothelial cells.
source: In addition, inactivation of Rb, which is induced by TNF-α treatment, has been shown to lead to various cellular behaviors including proliferation of vascular smooth muscle cells (Rastogi et al., 2012) and apoptosis of fibroblasts and aortic endothelial cells (Chau and Wang, 2003; Rastogi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Rastogi et al., 2012 and Chau and Wang, 2003.

claim: Rb at the mitochondria participates in TNF-α-induced apoptosis.
source: Recently, a non-nuclear function of Rb has been reported; where Rb at the mitochondria participates in TNF-α-induced apoptosis (Hilgendorf et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hilgendorf et al., 2013.

claim: A sarcomere is the basic functional unit of striated muscle and consists of two sets of filaments: thick and thin.
source: A sarcomere is the basic functional unit of striated muscle and consists of two sets of filaments: thick and thin (Squire, 1997; Gautel, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Squire, 1997 and Gautel, 2011.

claim: The thick filaments are composed of myosin proteins.
source: The thick filaments are composed of myosin proteins and the thin filaments are assembled from polymerized actin monomers, called filamentous actin (F-actin).
evidence: This is established knowledge about sarcomere structure.

claim: The thin filaments are assembled from polymerized actin monomers, called filamentous actin (F-actin).
source: The thick filaments are composed of myosin proteins and the thin filaments are assembled from polymerized actin monomers, called filamentous actin (F-actin).
evidence: This is established knowledge about sarcomere structure.

claim: The contractile activity of skeletal muscle is achieved through the actin and myosin filaments sliding past one another.
source: The contractile activity of skeletal muscle is achieved through the actin and myosin filaments sliding past one another (Squire, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Squire, 1997.

claim: The motor function of striated muscle requires the well-ordered assembly of sarcomeres, which is closely tied to the highly organized actin cytoskeleton.
source: The motor function of striated muscle therefore, requires the well-ordered assembly of sarcomeres, which is closely tied to the highly organized actin cytoskeleton.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about muscle structure and function.

claim: The formins are characterized by the presence of the conserved formin homology 2 (FH2) domain.
source: The formins are a large family of proteins and are characterized by the presence of the conserved formin homology 2 (FH2) domain (Kovar, 2006; Campellone and Welch, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kovar, 2006 and Campellone and Welch, 2010.

claim: The FH2 domain promotes actin nucleation and polymerization, thereby producing long straight actin filaments and regulating cytoskeletal organization.
source: The FH2 domain promotes actin nucleation and polymerization, thereby producing long straight actin filaments and regulating cytoskeletal organization.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about formin function.

claim: Several members of the formin family serve as key regulators of actin dynamics during sarcomeric organization in striated muscle.
source: It has been reported that several members of the formin family serve as key regulators of actin dynamics during sarcomeric organization in striated muscle (Taniguchi et al., 2009; Kan et al., 2012; Mi-Mi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Taniguchi et al., 2009; Kan et al., 2012; Mi-Mi et al., 2012.

claim: During differentiation from myoblasts to myotubes (from day 0 to day 4), Rb shifted from a phosphorylated to an unphosphorylated state.
source: During differentiation from myoblasts to myotubes (from day 0 to day 4), Rb shifted from a phosphorylated to an unphosphorylated state (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Following TNF-α treatment, Rb phosphorylation on the CDK4-specific phosphorylation site, serine 780, was induced.
source: Moreover, following TNF-α treatment Rb phosphorylation on the CDK4-specific phosphorylation site, serine 780 (Kitagawa et al., 1996), was induced (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and a citation to Kitagawa et al., 1996.

claim: Rb phosphorylation on threonine 821, a CDK2-specific phosphorylation site, was not observed after TNF-α treatment.
source: This was not observed on threonine 821, a CDK2-specific phosphorylation site (Halaban, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and a citation to Halaban, 2005.

claim: In untreated HSMMs, Rb was primarily present in the nucleus.
source: In untreated HSMMs, Rb was primarily present in the nucleus, but translocated to the cytoplasm after TNF-α treatment (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1B and 1C.

claim: Rb translocated to the cytoplasm after TNF-α treatment.
source: In untreated HSMMs, Rb was primarily present in the nucleus, but translocated to the cytoplasm after TNF-α treatment (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1B and 1C.

claim: Phosphorylated Rb in TNF-α-treated HSMMs was predominantly located in the cytoplasm.
source: In addition, we found that phosphorylated Rb in TNF-α-treated HSMMs was predominantly located in the cytoplasm (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: TNF-α treatment led to an increase in the level of nuclear CDK4.
source: In accordance with the induction of Rb phosphorylation on a CDK4-specific phosphorylation site, TNF-α treatment led to an increase in the level of nuclear CDK4 (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The vast majority of nuclear Rb was in an unphosphorylated state.
source: The vast majority of nuclear Rb was in an unphosphorylated state, while cytoplasmic Rb that accumulated after TNF-α treatment was in a phosphorylated state (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Cytoplasmic Rb that accumulated after TNF-α treatment was in a phosphorylated state.
source: The vast majority of nuclear Rb was in an unphosphorylated state, while cytoplasmic Rb that accumulated after TNF-α treatment was in a phosphorylated state (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: When CDK4 was depleted by short hairpin RNA (shRNA), cytoplasmic accumulation of Rb induced by TNF-α was decreased.
source: When CDK4 was depleted by short hairpin RNA (shRNA), cytoplasmic accumulation of Rb induced by TNF-α was decreased (Figure 1F–H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1F-H.

claim: Phosphorylation of Rb by CDK4 triggers its cytoplasmic translocation in HSMMs.
source: These results suggest that phosphorylation of Rb by CDK4 triggers its cytoplasmic translocation in HSMMs.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that CDK4 depletion prevents cytoplasmic accumulation of Rb.

claim: In human skeletal muscle myoblasts, Rb was mainly in a phosphorylated state.
source: In human skeletal muscle myoblasts, Rb was mainly in a phosphorylated state (Figure 1A, day 0), although the localization of S780-phosphorylated Rb was confined to the nucleus (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 2A.

claim: The localization of S780-phosphorylated Rb was confined to the nucleus in human skeletal muscle myoblasts.
source: In human skeletal muscle myoblasts, Rb was mainly in a phosphorylated state (Figure 1A, day 0), although the localization of S780-phosphorylated Rb was confined to the nucleus (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Lamina-associated polypeptide (LAP) 2α interacts with S780-phosphorylated Rb in mitotic myoblasts.
source: Lamina-associated polypeptide (LAP) 2α, a binding partner of nucleoplasmic A-type lamins, interacts with S780-phosphorylated Rb in mitotic myoblasts (Markiewicz et al., 2005) and is known to play an important role in nuclear tethering of Rb (Markiewicz et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Markiewicz et al., 2005 and Markiewicz et al., 2002.

claim: LAP2α plays an important role in nuclear tethering of Rb.
source: Lamina-associated polypeptide (LAP) 2α, a binding partner of nucleoplasmic A-type lamins, interacts with S780-phosphorylated Rb in mitotic myoblasts (Markiewicz et al., 2005) and is known to play an important role in nuclear tethering of Rb (Markiewicz et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Markiewicz et al., 2002.

claim: When LAP2α was depleted by shRNA in human myoblasts, Rb localized to the cytoplasm as well as the nucleus.
source: Indeed, when LAP2α was depleted by shRNA in human myoblasts, Rb localized to the cytoplasm as well as the nucleus (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The level of LAP2α decreased during muscle differentiation.
source: Given the level of LAP2α decreased during muscle differentiation (Markiewicz et al., 2005) (Figure 2C), these results suggest that low-level LAP2α expression in HSMMs facilitates the cytoplasmic translocation of Rb.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and a citation to Markiewicz et al., 2005.

claim: Low-level LAP2α expression in HSMMs facilitates the cytoplasmic translocation of Rb.
source: Given the level of LAP2α decreased during muscle differentiation (Markiewicz et al., 2005) (Figure 2C), these results suggest that low-level LAP2α expression in HSMMs facilitates the cytoplasmic translocation of Rb.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing LAP2α depletion causes Rb cytoplasmic localization and LAP2α decreases during differentiation.

claim: LAP2α is an E2F-target gene.
source: It has been reported that LAP2α is an E2F-target gene and its expression is enhanced in cancer cells (Parise et al., 2006; Ward et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Parise et al., 2006 and Ward et al., 2011.

claim: LAP2α expression is enhanced in cancer cells.
source: It has been reported that LAP2α is an E2F-target gene and its expression is enhanced in cancer cells (Parise et al., 2006; Ward et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Parise et al., 2006 and Ward et al., 2011.

claim: Overexpressed LAP2α may serve to tether Rb to the nucleus in cancer cells.
source: Overexpressed LAP2α may therefore serve to tether Rb to the nucleus in cancer cells and the cytoplasmic translocation of Rb may be triggered in cells that express low levels of LAP2α, such as terminally differentiated cells.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the experimental findings about LAP2α function.

claim: The cytoplasmic translocation of Rb may be triggered in cells that express low levels of LAP2α, such as terminally differentiated cells.
source: Overexpressed LAP2α may therefore serve to tether Rb to the nucleus in cancer cells and the cytoplasmic translocation of Rb may be triggered in cells that express low levels of LAP2α, such as terminally differentiated cells.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the experimental findings about LAP2α function.

claim: Approximately 55% of HSMMs displayed beating in response to electric pulse stimulation (EPS).
source: In response to electric pulse stimulation (EPS), which evokes a contractile reaction in myotubes (Fujita et al., 2007), approximately 55% of HSMMs displayed beating, an index of contractile reaction (Figure 3A; Video 1)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Beating was hardly observed after TNF-α treatment.
source: In response to electric pulse stimulation (EPS), which evokes a contractile reaction in myotubes (Fujita et al., 2007), approximately 55% of HSMMs displayed beating, an index of contractile reaction (Figure 3A; Video 1), while it was hardly observed after TNF-α treatment (Figure 3A; Video 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In untreated HSMMs, α-actinin was observed at evenly spaced intervals.
source: In untreated HSMMs, α-actinin was observed at evenly spaced intervals, whereas in TNF-α-treated HSMMs the peak-to-peak distance in line plots of α-actinin intensity along the myofibril was larger and inconsistent (Figure 3B–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3B-D.

claim: In TNF-α-treated HSMMs the peak-to-peak distance in line plots of α-actinin intensity along the myofibril was larger and inconsistent.
source: In untreated HSMMs, α-actinin was observed at evenly spaced intervals, whereas in TNF-α-treated HSMMs the peak-to-peak distance in line plots of α-actinin intensity along the myofibril was larger and inconsistent (Figure 3B–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3B-D.

claim: Peak values in autocorrelation analysis were much lower in TNF-α-treated HSMMs.
source: Furthermore, when the repeating pattern of α-actinin distribution was analyzed using an autocorrelation image processing technique, peak values were much lower in TNF-α-treated HSMMs (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The periodic assembly of sarcomeres is disrupted by TNF-α treatment.
source: These results indicate that the periodic assembly of sarcomeres is disrupted by TNF-α treatment.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing disrupted α-actinin distribution after TNF-α treatment.

claim: The peak-to-peak distance in line plots of α-actinin intensity reflects a counterbalance between tensile forces generated by the actin filaments.
source: In striated muscle cells, anti-parallel actin filaments spanning the sarcomeres are crosslinked to the Z-disks (Sparrow and Schock, 2009). The peak-to-peak distance in line plots of α-actinin intensity therefore reflects a counterbalance between tensile forces generated by the actin filaments.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about sarcomere structure and a citation to Sparrow and Schock, 2009.

claim: Sarcomeric disorganization represents an imbalance in the tensile forces, which may be caused by defective actin filament formation.
source: Sarcomeric disorganization represents an imbalance in the tensile forces, which may be caused by defective actin filament formation.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the understanding of sarcomere structure.

claim: After 30 min of cytochalasin D treatment, the periodic arrangement of α-actinin was not well ordered.
source: After 30 min of treatment, the periodic arrangement of α-actinin was not well ordered (Figure 4A–C) and was strongly disordered by 60 min (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4A-C.

claim: The periodic arrangement of α-actinin was strongly disordered by 60 min of cytochalasin D treatment.
source: After 30 min of treatment, the periodic arrangement of α-actinin was not well ordered (Figure 4A–C) and was strongly disordered by 60 min (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Rb is required for myogenic differentiation but not for the maintenance of the terminally differentiated state in myotubes.
source: Rb is known to be required for myogenic differentiation but not for the maintenance of the terminally differentiated state in myotubes (Huh et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Huh et al., 2004.

claim: Sarcomeric organization was not affected when Rb was depleted by shRNA.
source: In accordance with this, sarcomeric organization was not affected when Rb was depleted by shRNA (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: After TNF-α treatment, the periodic assembly of sarcomeres was disrupted in control shRNA-expressing HSMMs.
source: After TNF-α treatment, the periodic assembly of sarcomeres was disrupted in control shRNA-expressing HSMMs, but TNF-α failed to induce the sarcomeric disorganization in sh-Rb-expressing HSMMs (Figure 5D–F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5D-F.

claim: TNF-α failed to induce sarcomeric disorganization in sh-Rb-expressing HSMMs.
source: After TNF-α treatment, the periodic assembly of sarcomeres was disrupted in control shRNA-expressing HSMMs, but TNF-α failed to induce the sarcomeric disorganization in sh-Rb-expressing HSMMs (Figure 5D–F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5D-F.

claim: Sarcomeric organization was not well ordered in NES Rb-expressing HSMMs at low expression levels.
source: Under this condition, sarcomeric organization was not well ordered as in TNF-α-treated HSMMs (Figure 6B–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6B-D.

claim: The periodic arrangement of α-actinin was significantly disordered when higher levels of NES Rb were expressed in HSMMs.
source: When we expressed higher levels of NES Rb in HSMMs (Figure 6E,F), the periodic arrangement of α-actinin was significantly disordered when compared to mCherry-HA-Rb-expressing cells (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6E-G.

claim: Rb is involved in TNF-α-induced sarcomeric disorganization.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that Rb is involved in TNF-α-induced sarcomeric disorganization and TNF-α-induced cytoplasmic Rb may have a pivotal role in this process.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that Rb depletion prevents TNF-α-induced sarcomeric disorganization and NES Rb expression causes sarcomeric disorganization.

claim: TNF-α-induced cytoplasmic Rb may have a pivotal role in sarcomeric disorganization.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that Rb is involved in TNF-α-induced sarcomeric disorganization and TNF-α-induced cytoplasmic Rb may have a pivotal role in this process.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that NES Rb expression causes sarcomeric disorganization.

claim: Threonine 821/threonine 826 phosphorylation disrupts Rb binding to LXCXE motif-containing proteins.
source: Given that it has been reported that threonine 821/threonine 826 phosphorylation disrupts Rb binding to LXCXE motif-containing proteins (Knudsen and Wang, 1996; Dick and Rubin, 2013), we examined whether the function of cytoplasmic Rb is achieved through its interaction with LXCXE motif-containing proteins.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Knudsen and Wang, 1996 and Dick and Rubin, 2013.

claim: The inhibitory effect of NES Rb Δexon 22 on sarcomeric organization was less effective as compared to NES Rb-expressing HSMMs.
source: We introduced mCherry-HA-NES Rb lacking exon 22 (Rb Δexon 22), which is known to be an LXCXE-binding deficient mutant (Henley et al., 2010), into HSMMs and found that the inhibitory effect of NES Rb Δexon 22 on sarcomeric organization was less effective as compared to NES Rb-expressing HSMMs (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A and a citation to Henley et al., 2010.

claim: mDia1 contains the LXCXE motif in the GTPase binding domain (GBD).
source: Among the proteins identified, we focused on mammalian diaphanous-related formin 1 (mDia1), a potent actin nucleation factor (Watanabe et al., 1997), as the LXCXE motif is contained in the GTPase binding domain (GBD) of mDia1 (Figure 7B,C).
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 7B and a citation to Watanabe et al., 1997.

claim: Binding of mDia1 to Rb was abolished by deletion of the LXCXE motif.
source: Data from purified wild-type and LXCXE motif-deleted mutant mDia1 proteins (WT and ΔLXCXE) (Figure 7C) showed that binding of mDia1 to Rb was abolished by deletion of the LXCXE motif (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Cytoplasmic Rb, which was phosphorylated and accumulated after TNF-α treatment, interacted with mDia1.
source: Cytoplasmic Rb, which was phosphorylated and accumulated after TNF-α treatment, interacted with mDia1 (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Unphosphorylated Rb protein containing the large pocket bound to mDia1 in vitro.
source: Unphosphorylated Rb protein containing the large pocket, an important domain for interactions with a variety of cellular proteins (Burkhart and Sage, 2008), bound to mDia1 in vitro and the binding level was strongly reduced according to its phosphorylation catalyzed by cyclin D/CDK4 and cyclin E/CDK2 complexes (Figure 7F,G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 7F and 7G and a citation to Burkhart and Sage, 2008.

claim: The binding level of Rb to mDia1 was strongly reduced according to its phosphorylation catalyzed by cyclin D/CDK4 and cyclin E/CDK2 complexes.
source: Unphosphorylated Rb protein containing the large pocket, an important domain for interactions with a variety of cellular proteins (Burkhart and Sage, 2008), bound to mDia1 in vitro and the binding level was strongly reduced according to its phosphorylation catalyzed by cyclin D/CDK4 and cyclin E/CDK2 complexes (Figure 7F,G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 7F and 7G.

claim: The mutant Rb bearing serine/threonine-to-alanine substitutions in the CDK2-specific phosphorylation sites exhibited substantial interaction with mDia1 even after phosphorylation.
source: We then tested a mutant Rb protein bearing serine/threonine-to-alanine substitutions in the CDK2-specific phosphorylation sites, serine 612 and threonine 821 (Mut CDK2). The mutant Rb exhibited substantial interaction with mDia1 even after phosphorylation (Figure 7G)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7G.

claim: Phosphorylation of Rb on CDK4 phosphorylation sites alone does not impair its interaction with mDia1.
source: The mutant Rb exhibited substantial interaction with mDia1 even after phosphorylation (Figure 7G), suggesting that phosphorylation of Rb on CDK4 phosphorylation sites alone does not impair its interaction with mDia1 and TNF-α-induced cytoplasmic Rb has the potential to interact with mDia1.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that the CDK2 mutant Rb retains binding to mDia1 after phosphorylation.

claim: TNF-α-induced cytoplasmic Rb has the potential to interact with mDia1.
source: The mutant Rb exhibited substantial interaction with mDia1 even after phosphorylation (Figure 7G), suggesting that phosphorylation of Rb on CDK4 phosphorylation sites alone does not impair its interaction with mDia1 and TNF-α-induced cytoplasmic Rb has the potential to interact with mDia1.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that CDK4-phosphorylated Rb can still bind mDia1.

claim: Muscle wasting/atrophy accompanies cancer-related skeletal muscle degeneration.
source: Muscle wasting/atrophy accompanies cancer-related skeletal muscle degeneration (Tisdale, 2002; Acharyya et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tisdale, 2002 and Acharyya et al., 2004.

claim: In normal muscles, Z-disks were regularly aligned and the sarcomere striation pattern was clearly observed.
source: In normal muscles, Z-disks were regularly aligned and the sarcomere striation pattern was clearly observed (Figure 8B, left).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: In atrophied muscles, the Z-disks were misaligned and the sarcomeric banding pattern was not well organized.
source: In contrast, the Z-disks were misaligned and the sarcomeric banding pattern was not well organized in the atrophied muscles (Figure 8B, right).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Rb was mainly located in the nucleus in normal muscle cells.
source: With regard to the localization of Rb, it was mainly located in the nucleus in normal muscle cells, but Rb could be observed in the cytoplasm, as well as the nucleus in atrophied muscle cells (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Rb could be observed in the cytoplasm, as well as the nucleus in atrophied muscle cells.
source: With regard to the localization of Rb, it was mainly located in the nucleus in normal muscle cells, but Rb could be observed in the cytoplasm, as well as the nucleus in atrophied muscle cells (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The localization of mDia1 was mainly confined to the Z-disk in both normal and atrophied skeletal muscles.
source: In both normal and atrophied skeletal muscles, the localization of mDia1 was mainly confined to the Z-disk (Figure 8B), and cytoplasmic Rb observed in atrophied muscles colocalized with mDia1 (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Cytoplasmic Rb observed in atrophied muscles colocalized with mDia1.
source: In both normal and atrophied skeletal muscles, the localization of mDia1 was mainly confined to the Z-disk (Figure 8B), and cytoplasmic Rb observed in atrophied muscles colocalized with mDia1 (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: mDia1 ΔGBD/ΔDAD itself did not affect either α-actinin distribution or the contractile reaction of HSMMs.
source: mDia1 ΔGBD/ΔDAD itself did not affect either α-actinin distribution or the contractile reaction of HSMMs (Figure 9B,C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 9B and 9C.

claim: After TNF-α treatment, the lateral alignment of α-actinin in GFP-mDia1 ΔGBD/ΔDAD-expressing HSMMs was well ordered as compared to that in control GFP-expressing HSMMs.
